A: On fully autonomous weapons, the logic as I understand it, it is not so much about democratic values. It's more that you think the technology is not ready for your models to be used fully autonomously. Is that right? So you have a different view of the capabilities of the technology perhaps than the Department of War.
B: Yeah, I think there's actually two things. One is this issue that you just mentioned, which is you can think of this as like a supplier of aircraft who says this aircraft is not safe to fly above a certain altitude or to turn at a certain speed. We didn't make these systems to be safe if you use them in that particular way, right? They're not suitable for this use case. Like, we haven't made them or manufactured them to work well, to be safe for this use case.
A: And in that, was there anything specific? I mean, your model has been used, was used in Venezuela, it's being used in Iran. Is there anything in these existing use cases that has worried you?
B: So one thing I want to say is we started with a substantially more limited contract that enabled a more limited number of use cases that I think is in force maybe even until today. This was all about negotiating a new contract. So we had even a substantially more limited contract for quite a long time, and that more limited contract they didn't run into problems with it on the ground. So none of this was driven by we have concerns right now about what the Department of War was doing, right?
A: Iran is fine and Venezuela was fine.
B: Again, I'm not expressing an opinion either way on military policy or government policy.
A: No, no, the use of your model. Yeah, use of your model.
B: If you provide a service You don't get to decide where that service is used. There's this operational side of military decisions. Of course, we don't have any say about that. What we do have say over is this question of like very broad use cases, right? It's not about any administration. It's not about any policy. It's like, how should this technology be used in general? I actually think there's a lot of value here. And, you know, I want to make sure the Department of War understands this as well. This isn't about, Concerns we have about actions they've taken or already taken. Like we had a much more limited contract. We never had concerns about this contract. This is about going forward. How should we think about the uses and the governance of this technology?
A: I think going forward, their perspective would be, and they would probably use the analogy of a fighter jet or something. And they would say, listen, we have to have suppliers who we can trust. and they provide us with tools that we can use in combat. And we can't have some guy in Silicon Valley suddenly saying, 'No, you can't use it for this, that, or the other.' And their view would be they need to have full operational ability to use it. And you are somewhat capriciously, in their view, putting all of these constraints on it.
B: Yeah. So I would say we agree with them. We don't wanna do that. We agree on 99%, not only the contract, we were operating on together. We agree on this much broader set of things that we haven't even done yet or are just starting to do. So I just wanna say again, there's so much more agreement here than there is disagreement.
A: [Speaker] I mean, listening to you, it does seem to me extraordinary that you end up in this situation where you're going to be taken out of all work with the Pentagon. That said, the other, 'cause I've been thinking about this quite a lot, the logical conclusion of total control by the Pentagon and no ability for the supplier to do anything is surely some sort of effective nationalization of those AI companies that work with the Pentagon. Do you think that's a risk?
B: I think over the coming years, we're going to have to have a discussion about the role of AI and the government. You know, AI is becoming something that has implications at the level of all of humanity. Not for national security in the sense of the contest between nations, for national security in the sense of can individuals use this technology for destruction, for national security in the sense of are the models themselves a risk to national security, for economics in terms of their impacts. And it's not about one particular administration, it's not about one particular department, it's not about specific military operations. Anyone who thinks that this is what that's about, that's a misunderstanding. This is bigger than that. This is big. This is about the next administration too. This is about, you know, Congress when there's different Congress people. This is about, you know, a different geopolitical situation that we're in than the one we're in now. It's, you know, we should not make it about what's happening right now. And the thing we're dealing with here is, AI is very powerful. So there's actually a dual dilemma here where AI has the power to make private actors more powerful than they've ever been before. Folks have— some people have criticized me for that. You think as a private actor you're more powerful than government. Actually, I've been worried about the risk of that for the longest time. Like, I'm worried about that. This technology abstractly in the hands of government not just the US government, other governments, democratic governments, autocratic governments, has the ability to vest them with unprecedented power as well. And so when we talked about fully autonomous weapons, I said there were two objections. The first one I said was reliability. The second one I said was what I would call oversight. And this is the idea that, you know, right now you have an army of human soldiers. And there are norms about serving in the military. You're supposed to follow orders, but if something crazy enough happened, the soldiers would say, "I'm not going to do that," right? Basically, you have a bunch of norms about how soldiers serve, right? What they see their duties to be. What if you have an army of 10 million drones instead of 10 million human soldiers? What are the norms of the AI-driven drones I think if we handle this wrongly, you could have a situation where there's a very small number of people, or one person, who has their hand on the button and kind of, you know, controls those 10 million drones. And we need to answer these questions because we don't want to make companies more powerful than the government, but we also don't want to make government so powerful that it can't be stopped. We have both problems at once.
A: Yeah. So you basically just said to me this technology is too powerful to be in the hands of a few private companies. And it's too powerful to be in the hands of a government.
B: That is unfortunately the situation we're in.
